definition: The perceived benefit received relative to the cost paid for a software product or service.
extendedDefinition: Value for money measures the benefit an organization receives relative to what it pays, and it is the real question behind every software purchase even when price dominates the conversation. It is not the same as lowest cost: an expensive tool that delivers measurable gains can outperform a cheap one that fails. Evaluating value for money requires articulating benefits in concrete terms, such as time saved, error reduction, revenue gained, or risk avoided, and comparing those against total cost of ownership including implementation and training. Per-seat versus usage-based pricing changes the calculation at different organization sizes, so value should be modeled at realistic adoption levels. Buyers should also consider indirect value like user satisfaction and compliance posture, which do not appear on invoices. The most defensible procurement decisions define the expected benefit before shortlisting and then measure whether the selected product delivers it.
examples: A team compares two project tools using annual subscription fees plus migration and training costs, then estimates hours saved using its expected number of active users.
A low-cost support platform requires manual reporting every week, so the buyer includes staff time in the comparison rather than judging subscription price alone.
Before renewal, a department checks whether the software achieved the original target—such as reducing ticket handling time—and whether the benefit still justifies the current price.
description: Value for money compares the practical benefit of software with its full cost. Learn how to include adoption, implementation, support, and measurable outcomes instead of choosing by sticker price alone.
